content: 1. There is likely no significant uncertainty or variability in the evidence regarding the balance of effects between universal screening and risk-based screening for Group B Streptococcus (GBS) in pregnant women. Universal screening is probably favored over risk-based screening in this context. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends screening pregnant women for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent early-onset GBS disease in newborns. When comparing universal screening with combined or other screening strategies, the evidence varies, and no definitive conclusion can be drawn. 3. A systematic review of the cost-effectiveness of GBS screening strategies identified one high-quality study conducted in the USA. This study focused on women with singleton pregnancies undergoing repeat cesarean births and found that universal screening was not cost-effective in this population. Sensitivity analyses indicated that universal screening would only become cost-effective if more than 28% of women were GBS-positive, more than 29% went into labor before their scheduled delivery, or more than 10% had vaginal births. 4. Another high-quality study conducted in the Netherlands reported incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) for universal screening compared to no screening and for risk-based screening compared to no screening. Risk-based screening was found to be cost-effective at $8,200 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained, while universal screening was not determined to be cost-effective at $64,482 per QALY gained. 5. The implementation of GBS screening requires resources such as laboratory facilities for swab testing, alcohol wipes, IV catheters, tubing, IV poles, and access to antibiotics like penicillin or ampicillin. Laboratory processing times can vary from several hours to several days, depending on the methods used and sample transportation times. 6. The feasibility of implementing intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) is limited in settings with a lack of skilled intrapartum care, higher rates of home births, or inadequate access to refrigeration for heat-sensitive antibiotics. Penicillin and ampicillin are listed in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. 7. A rapid review of stakeholder perceptions found that most women (at least 80%) find GBS swabbing acceptable, with moderate confidence in the evidence. However, some women report negative views due to embarrassment, fear of altered birth plans, overmedicalization, and concerns about implications for the baby. 8. Younger women are less likely to find vaginal and rectal swabbing acceptable compared to older women. Ethnicity may also influence the acceptability of GBS testing, though research is limited. Obstetricians are more likely to discuss and follow GBS screening policies than nursing and midwifery professionals. 9. Most health professionals view GBS screening as important and beneficial for pregnant women. However, midwives are generally opposed to universal antibiotic use, while obstetricians may find it more acceptable. There is no clear evidence on whether universal or risk-based screening is more acceptable to health professionals. 10. Barriers to GBS screening and prophylaxis include organizational challenges, fear of consequences such as maternal anxiety and overmedicalization, lack of clarity in guidelines, medicolegal concerns, and insufficient training. Facilitators include patient requests, the presence of guidelines, adherence to guidelines among peers, and personal experiences with GBS. 11. The acceptability of self-swabbing versus swabbing by a healthcare professional varies. Women value the comfort, privacy, and control of self-swabbing but may feel more confident in the accuracy of swabbing performed by a professional. Vaginal swabbing is generally more acceptable than rectal swabbing. 12. The evidence on the cost-effectiveness of universal screening compared to risk-based screening is uncertain. Risk-based screening is likely more cost-effective, but further research is needed to confirm this. 13. The impact of GBS screening on health equity is unclear. Women who are poor, less educated, or living in rural areas are less likely to have access to GBS testing and IAP, which are typically available only for facility births. 14. Clear communication and provision of information are critical to mitigating maternal anxiety and ensuring informed decision-making regarding GBS screening and prophylaxis.
